summary: This Standards Track document defines a mechanism for a bootstrapping device and a TLS server to authenticate each other. The device has a key pair; the server proves it knows the device's public key and the device proves it holds the private key. It builds on the Device Provisioning Profile and existing TLS.

eli5.summary: Two strangers meet. One knows what the other's key looks like, and the other can show they truly own that key.

questions: tls with proof of knowledge of public key
how does bootstrapped tls authentication work
what is a bootstrap key bsk
subtitle: How a brand-new device and a TLS server prove to each other that they know the device's key, before any credential exists.

tldr.problem: A device with no screen and no credential needs network access, but getting a credential needs network access. The device also has little way to check that the network it joins is the right one.
tldr.mechanism: TLS-POK derives a TLS 1.3 external pre-shared key from the device's public key, so the server proves it knows that key. The device then proves it holds the private key by authenticating with that key as a raw public key.
tldr.outcome: Both sides are mutually authenticated, and over EAP (using TEAP) the server can go on to provision a credential. It is a Proposed Standard, intended for wired 802.1X networks rather than wireless ones.

today: RFC 9966 is a Proposed Standard, published in May 2026, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It depends on the eap.arpa identity mechanism of RFC 9965 and on TEAP in RFC 9930.

sections.title: The Bootstrapping Problem
sections.content:
Devices with little or no user interface are hard to onboard. A network protected by 802.1X or EAP wants a credential, yet the device needs network connectivity to obtain one. If the device has a public/private key pair and trust in its public key can be obtained out of band, the device can be authenticated and given a usable credential. That authentication of the device can be strong, but the device's authentication of the network is somewhat weaker.

Existing onboarding protocols such as the Device Provisioning Profile (DPP, also called Wi-Fi Easy Connect) address this, but DPP does not support wired network access and does not say how the device's DPP key pair is used in a TLS handshake. RFC 9966 defines TLS Proof of Knowledge (TLS-POK) for that gap, including its use in an EAP exchange for wired access.

The RFC says TLS-POK SHOULD NOT be used to bootstrap against wireless networks and SHOULD be used against wired networks. It does not address wireless network discovery.
sections.eli5: A new gadget needs a pass to enter the building, but the pass desk is inside the building. This is a way to get the gadget in the door the first time.

sections.title: The Bootstrap Key
sections.content:
The device holds an elliptic curve key pair called the Bootstrap Key (BSK), from a cryptosystem suitable for ECDSA. The private key is known only to the device. The public key is known by the device, known by the owner or holder of the device, and provisioned on the TLS server by the server operator. The BSK may be baked into firmware at manufacture or generated by the device at onboarding time.

The public key MUST be encoded as the DER representation of an ASN.1 SubjectPublicKeyInfo SEQUENCE, including the AlgorithmIdentifier, and the subjectPublicKey MUST be in compressed format.

How the server learns the public key is out of scope. The RFC gives examples: scanning a QR code carrying a base64 encoding of the DER, or uploading a Bill of Materials. The model assumes that physical possession of the device implies legitimate ownership.

The encoding aligns with DPP, so one QR code on a label can serve DPP on Wi-Fi and TLS-POK on a wired network. DPP, and therefore TLS-POK, does not support RSA or postquantum systems because of the size of the public key and its unsuitability for a QR code.
sections.eli5: The device has a secret stamp and a picture of the stamp's pattern. The pattern is printed on a sticker, so the owner can tell the building about it ahead of time.

sections.title: Deriving the External PSK
sections.content:
TLS-POK uses TLS 1.3 certificate-based authentication with an external pre-shared key (EPSK), imported as described in RFC 9258. The EPSK is the tuple of Base Key, External Identity and Hash. The Base Key is the DER-encoded SubjectPublicKeyInfo of the BSK public key, with no zero-byte padding added.

The External Identity, epskid, is computed with HKDF (RFC 5869) using SHA-256, with the label tls13-bspsk-identity, a length L of 32 and a null salt. SHA-256 MUST be used for this derivation.

The ImportedIdentity structure then carries external_identity = epskid, context = "tls13-bsk", a target_protocol of TLS 1.3 (0x0304) and a target_kdf that follows RFC 9258. The context value MUST be tls13-bsk; it tells the server that this document's mechanisms apply.

A server can precompute the identity of every bootstrapped key for every hash it uses and look keys up quickly, or skip that storage and check each key it holds at runtime.
sections.eli5: Both sides turn the public key into a secret password and a nickname using the same recipe. The nickname goes on the wire; the password never does.

sections.title: The TLS 1.3 Handshake
sections.content:
The client sends the tls_cert_with_extern_psk extension (RFC 8773) in its ClientHello, puts the serialized ImportedIdentity in the PSK identity, and MUST include the client_certificate_type extension (RFC 7250) specifying RawPublicKey. If the server finds no matching key it MUST end the handshake with an alert. If it does, it echoes the extensions, and the key schedule MUST mix in both the EPSK and a (EC)DHE shared secret.

The server MUST send a CertificateRequest, and the client MUST authenticate with its BSK as a raw ECDSA public key. The server MUST check that the key in the client's Certificate is identical to the one it used to build the EPSK and ImportedIdentity.

The client MUST NOT send its BSK public key until it has processed the ServerHello and verified the key schedule. If the PSK check fails, the client ends the handshake and the key MUST NOT be shared.

A client that trusts the first network proving knowledge of its key MAY skip checking the server's certificate in CertificateVerify.
sections.eli5: The server shows it knows the secret first. Only after the device is satisfied does it reveal its own stamp. Nobody shows their card to a stranger.

sections.title: Using TLS-POK in EAP
sections.content:
When a link comes up on an 802.1X port, the Authenticator sends an EAP Identity request. An unprovisioned device has no realm to build a Network Access Identifier from, so RFC 9966 uses the mechanism in RFC 9965 and defines the username tls-pok-dpp for the TEAP realm teap.eap.arpa. The identity tls-pok-dpp@teap.eap.arpa MUST be sent in the EAP Identity response, which signals that TEAP is the wanted method.

The client then starts TLS inside TEAP with the ImportedIdentity in the ClientHello. After the handshake completes, the two sides have mutual trust and the server can provision a credential, for example using TEAP (RFC 9930). The BSK is used only during bootstrap, not for later EAP authentication.

TEAP is the only EAP method assumed, because it is the only one that currently supports provisioning a certificate to a device.
sections.eli5: The device introduces itself with a special first-time name. That name tells the network to use the guest-welcome routine, and afterwards the device gets a proper badge.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The server's trust rests on proof that the client holds the private key matching a non-public public key. The client's trust rests on the server proving, through the EPSK, that it knows that public key, which the client assumes is not widely disseminated.

The RFC lists limits. Substituting a rogue device's public key for an honest one during bootstrapping can get the rogue device onboarded. An adversary who learns the public key, for instance by scanning QR labels, and can force the client to connect to its server can complete the handshake. A stolen device can still be onboarded because possession implies ownership. The BSK public key MUST NOT be freely available on the network.

The key pair MUST be generated and validated per Section 6.2 of NIST FIPS 186-5, and manufacturers SHOULD use a unique BSK for every device, otherwise operators cannot tell devices apart.
sections.eli5: It only works if the sticker with the pattern stays private. If a stranger copies it, they could pretend to be the doorman.
